title: Weighting: Fixing a Lopsided Sample
objective: After this level you can explain how pollsters weight answers so a sample's mix of ages and backgrounds matches the population.
summary: Pollsters weight answers so a sample's mix of age, sex, race, education and region matches Census figures. Weighting fixes the mix, not traits it doesn't measure, and widens the margin.

cards.headline: Your poll has too few young adults. Now what?
cards.body: No sample comes out a perfect miniature of the country, because some people are simply easier to reach. So pollsters do the next best thing: they make some answers count more than others.

cards.headline: Easy to reach, overcounted
cards.body: Left alone, polls overrepresent people who are easier to reach and underrepresent those who are harder to interview. So after the answers come in, pollsters weight them. Gallup, for example, gives each respondent a weight so the sample's mix of gender, race, age, education and region matches the Census Bureau's latest estimates.

cards.headline: Counting some voices double
cards.body: Say young adults are 20% of the population but only 10% of your sample. Each young adult's answers then count about twice, and overrepresented groups count a little less, until the mix matches. Doing this for several traits, one after another until they all line up, is called raking. It's the standard method at Pew and many other pollsters.

cards.fact: Weighting fixes the mix, not the mindset.
cards.context: It can only balance the traits a pollster weights on. Remember Level 56's volunteers: standard weighting falls short when polls measure volunteering, so those estimates stay too high. And weighting has a price: it makes the margin of error bigger.

mascot.line: If you remember one thing: weighting can balance who answered, not why they answered.

cards.headline: Weighting: fixing the mix
learned: Raking: one trait at a time

questions.prompt: Young adults are underrepresented in your poll. Match each with its number.
questions.explanation: Young adults are 20% of the population but only 10% of your sample, so each young adult's answers count about twice until the mix matches.

questions.prompt: Why doesn't weighting fix Pew's overcount of volunteers?

options.label: Volunteers refuse to give their age
options.rationale: They answer fine; the problem is why they answer.

options.label: Weighting only works on very small samples, and Pew's samples are large
options.rationale: Weighting is used on samples of every size.

options.label: There are no Census figures for age
options.rationale: There are; that's what pollsters weight to.

options.label: Balancing traits like age can't fix a bias tied to volunteering itself

questions.explanation: Weighting balances the traits it uses. Volunteers answer more because they volunteer, so standard weighting falls short.

questions.prompt: Weighting mainly answers which polling problem?

options.label: Some kinds of people answer surveys less often
Questions worded to push an answer
options.rationale: Weighting can't change how a question was asked.

options.label: Margins reported in points instead of in percent
options.rationale: That's just the unit, not a problem to fix.

options.label: Robocalls ringing too often
options.rationale: Weighting adjusts answers; it can't stop calls.

questions.explanation: Nonresponse leaves some groups underrepresented; weighting counts their answers more so the mix matches the population.
